note: The attacker-controlled testcase is injected into the client's input BIO and becomes handshake traffic.
The injected bytes drive the TLS client state machine and parsing of server handshake messages.
Before processing a new key exchange, the client drops any previous temporary peer key reference.
A DH object is allocated to hold the server's advertised finite-field parameters and public key.
The peer public key is parsed from attacker-controlled bytes and validated as non-zero before use.
Ownership of the DH object is transferred into an EVP_PKEY wrapper that will later free it via the DH destructor.
The attacker-influenced temporary peer key is stored in SSL state for subsequent handshake and teardown logic.
When the SSL object is finalized, the temporary peer key is released through EVP_PKEY_free.
The EVP_PKEY reference count is decremented and, on the last release, control enters the type-specific destructor path.
The DH wrapper destructor frees the embedded DH object held by the EVP_PKEY.
The DH reference count is decremented; the final release proceeds to free the DH internals.
The DH structure itself is deallocated, completing the cleanup path that can expose a stale owner to later use.
